task_2.title: Fix error handler typing compatibility
task_2.description: The 2.0.3 update fixes Flask's public type annotations for error handler registration so valid handlers passed to the errorhandler decorator or register_error_handler no longer fail static type checking. This restores expected typing behavior for handlers that accept an exception instance and return a normal Flask response value.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that registering an error handler for exceptions is accepted by static type checkers when the handler takes the declared exception type and returns a valid Flask response value.

expectation.grounded: The public typing for Flask error-handler registration must treat ErrorHandlerCallable as a callable that accepts the registered exception type and returns ResponseReturnValue. This must allow correctly typed handlers used with app.errorhandler(...) and app.register_error_handler(...), including broad handlers such as Exception and HTTP exception subclasses, without requiring casts or incompatible-type workarounds.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to declare error handlers in the normal Flask style and have valid signatures pass type checking. A handler that receives the exception object and returns a standard Flask response should be recognized as compatible when registered for that exception type.

constraints.grounded: The change must be limited to typing behavior and must not alter runtime error-handling registration or response generation semantics. Registered handlers must still be modeled as single-argument callables returning valid Flask response values, and existing valid exception-specific handler signatures must remain accepted.
constraints.conceptual: This update should improve developer tooling compatibility without changing how error handlers behave at runtime. Existing correctly written handlers should continue to work, and broader exception handlers should not lose compatibility.

behavior: Static typing for Flask error handlers recognizes a handler as compatible when it accepts the registered exception type and returns a Flask response value.
Using @app.errorhandler(...) with a correctly typed handler for Exception or a specific exception type no longer produces an incompatible callable type solely because of Flask's annotation.
Using app.register_error_handler(...) with the same class of correctly typed handler is subject to the same corrected callable typing.
The change affects type-checking and editor/static-analysis behavior only; runtime registration and execution behavior remain unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer registers an error handler for Exception and the handler signature is (Exception) -> ResponseReturnValue, static type checking should accept the registration.

When a developer registers an error handler for a specific exception class and the handler accepts that exception type and returns a valid Flask response value, static type checking should accept the registration.
When the same handler is registered through either the decorator form or the explicit register_error_handler API, both forms should be treated consistently by type checkers.
Upgrading to 2.0.3 should not change the runtime behavior of error handling; the improvement should be limited to type annotation compatibility.

task_3.title: Restore Flask CLI ImportError Tracebacks During App Loading
task_3.description: Flask 2.0.3 restores CLI visibility into application import failures by surfacing the original ImportError traceback when the app module imports successfully but one of its internal imports fails. The CLI should still keep the simpler missing-module error path for cases where the requested app module itself cannot be imported.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the Flask CLI shows actionable import failure details when loading an application raises an ImportError from inside the application or one of its dependencies, while continuing to distinguish that case from a missing application module.

expectation.grounded: When the Flask CLI imports an application module, `locate_app` should raise `NoAppException` with the original `ImportError` traceback included when the `ImportError` occurs from within the imported module or a dependency loaded during that import. If the requested module itself cannot be imported and `raise_if_not_found` is enabled, the CLI should continue to raise `NoAppException` indicating that the module could not be imported, without treating it as an internal application traceback case.
expectation.conceptual: Using the Flask CLI to load an app should expose enough traceback information to identify the real missing or broken import inside the app startup path. A genuinely missing app module should still produce the normal module-not-found style failure instead of being reported as an internal app import traceback.

constraints.grounded: Preserve the existing separation between a target module that cannot be imported at all and an `ImportError` raised after import execution has entered the target module. Do not change successful app discovery behavior or convert all import failures into the same user-visible error form.
constraints.conceptual: Keep current successful CLI loading behavior unchanged, and only expand error detail for the specific regression where internal import failures became opaque. Distinct categories of import failure should remain distinguishable to the user.

behavior: If the Flask CLI encounters an `ImportError` while executing imports inside the target application module, it reports the failure through `NoAppException` and includes the formatted traceback of the original import failure.
If the target application module itself cannot be imported, the Flask CLI continues to raise `NoAppException` indicating that the module could not be imported.
The CLI distinguishes between nested import failures inside app loading and top-level inability to import the requested module name.
acceptance_criteria: When an application module imports successfully enough to begin execution but a dependency import inside that module raises `ImportError`, running a Flask CLI command should fail with a `NoAppException` that includes traceback details for the underlying import failure.

When the named application module does not exist or cannot be imported as the requested module, running a Flask CLI command should fail with the existing module-could-not-import style `NoAppException` rather than an internal traceback-style import error report.
When application loading succeeds without import failures, Flask CLI app discovery and command execution should behave as before.

task_1.title: Deprecate Flask test client as_tuple usage
task_1.description: Flask 2.0.3 updates its test client to stay compatible with the deprecation and removal of Werkzeug's `as_tuple` parameter. Explicit `as_tuple` usage is still accepted in the 2.0.x line, but it now raises a deprecation warning and users are directed to read the request environ from `response.request.environ` instead.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask's test client continues to work for applications upgrading to 2.0.3 while phasing out the deprecated `as_tuple` usage, and ensure callers can access request environment data through the response object instead of relying on tuple returns.

expectation.grounded: Flask's test client, via `FlaskClient.open` and request helper methods that delegate to it, should keep accepting an explicitly provided `as_tuple` keyword during the Flask 2.0.x series for compatibility with existing callers. Any explicit `as_tuple` usage should emit a `DeprecationWarning`. Calls that do not provide `as_tuple` should return a `TestResponse` object through the normal response path. The supported replacement for accessing the WSGI environ is `response.request.environ` on the returned response object.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading to Flask 2.0.3, existing test client code that still passes `as_tuple` should keep working temporarily, but it should clearly warn that this pattern is deprecated and scheduled for removal. Normal test client calls should behave as standard response-returning calls, and code that needs request environment details should read them from the response object.

constraints.grounded: Do not break existing 2.0.x callers solely because they pass `as_tuple`; preserve compatibility by forwarding that argument when it is explicitly supplied. Do not emit the deprecation warning for calls that omit `as_tuple`. Preserve existing `buffered` and `follow_redirects` request behavior while changing only the handling of the deprecated parameter.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should be backward-compatible for current users during the 2.0.x line, while only warning on deprecated usage and leaving unrelated test client behavior unchanged.

behavior: Explicitly providing the `as_tuple` keyword to the Flask test client triggers a `DeprecationWarning`.
If `as_tuple` is not provided, the Flask test client follows the standard response path and returns a response object rather than using tuple compatibility behavior.
Temporary compatibility for explicit `as_tuple` usage is retained in Flask 2.0.3 so existing callers are not immediately broken before Flask 2.1.
The supported way to obtain request environ data from a test client call is through `response.request.environ`.
acceptance_criteria: When a Flask test client request is made without `as_tuple`, it should return a normal response object and should not emit the new deprecation warning.
When a Flask test client request explicitly passes `as_tuple`, it should still complete in Flask 2.0.3 and emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating that the parameter is deprecated.
When transitional code uses `as_tuple=True`, the call should remain compatible during the 2.0.x line rather than failing immediately.
When application code needs the request environ after a test client call, it should be able to access it from `response.request.environ` instead of relying on tuple unpacking.

task_4.title: Avoid no-op JSON hook overrides in default Flask JSON handling
task_4.description: Flask 2.0.3 reduces overhead in JSON serialization and deserialization by only applying app or blueprint JSON encoder and decoder class overrides when they introduce custom behavior. Default JSON handling should keep the same results while using a faster standard path, especially for large payloads and PyPy.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask's default JSON serialization and deserialization path does not pay extra overhead for encoder or decoder hook classes when no custom JSON behavior has been configured, while still honoring custom JSON handling defined by the application or blueprint.

expectation.grounded: When `flask.json.dumps` and `flask.json.loads` resolve JSON hook classes from `app.json_encoder`, `app.json_decoder`, or blueprint-specific overrides, they should only pass a `cls` override to the underlying JSON library when that class changes behavior from the normal default implementation. If the resolved decoder is Flask's default `JSONDecoder` or the standard library decoder, `loads` should use the default decoder path. Custom encoder or decoder classes configured by the app or active blueprint must continue to be applied.
expectation.conceptual: Flask JSON helpers should use the normal fast path when the application has not customized JSON encoding or decoding, and should only activate custom JSON class behavior when the application explicitly provides it.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress support for custom JSON encoder or decoder classes configured on the application or blueprint. Default JSON parsing and dumping behavior should remain compatible with existing Flask behavior, except that unnecessary no-op class injection should be removed from the default path.
constraints.conceptual: Keep existing customized JSON behavior intact, and do not change normal JSON results other than removing avoidable overhead from the default configuration.

behavior: `flask.json.loads` should no longer force a decoder class when the resolved decoder is equivalent to Flask's default `JSONDecoder` or the standard library decoder.
`flask.json.dumps` should only supply an encoder class override when the resolved encoder introduces behavior beyond the standard/default encoder path.
If a custom JSON decoder or encoder is configured on the app or active blueprint, Flask JSON helpers should continue to use that custom class.
Default Flask JSON operations should avoid unnecessary class-based dispatch overhead, improving performance for large JSON payloads, particularly on PyPy.
acceptance_criteria: When an application uses the default Flask JSON decoder configuration, loading JSON through Flask's JSON helpers should follow the standard decoder path instead of forcing a no-op decoder class override.
When an application or blueprint provides a custom JSON decoder, Flask JSON loading should continue to apply that decoder.
When an application uses the default JSON encoder and decoder behavior, JSON helper calls should preserve existing JSON results while avoiding the prior unnecessary hook-class overhead.
When large JSON payloads are processed through Flask's normal JSON helper path, the default configuration should benefit from the performance improvement without requiring application code changes.

task_5.title: Clarify request-context misuse errors for request decorators
task_5.description: Version 2.0.3 improves developer-facing runtime behavior when request-scoped decorators are used outside an active request. `after_this_request` now fails with an intentional request-context error instead of an incidental attribute error, and the related `copy_current_request_context` guidance is made consistent and clearer.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that request-scoped decorators report a clear runtime error when they are used without an active request context.

expectation.grounded: When `after_this_request` is used without an active request context, it should raise `RuntimeError` explaining that the decorator is only valid while a request context is active, such as within a view function, instead of failing with an unrelated attribute-access exception. `copy_current_request_context` should present the same request-context requirement and `RuntimeError` semantics when no active request context exists.
expectation.conceptual: If a developer accidentally uses request-only decorators outside a live request, the library should fail with a clear, actionable runtime error that explains the misuse and the valid context for using it.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the normal successful behavior of `after_this_request` or `copy_current_request_context` when a request context is active. Preserve the existing public APIs and keep missing-context failures in the `RuntimeError` category rather than introducing a new exception type.
constraints.conceptual: Correct in-request usage should continue to behave as before. The update should only improve the clarity and consistency of failure behavior for out-of-context calls.

behavior: `after_this_request` now validates that a request context is active before registering its callback.
Calling `after_this_request` outside a request context raises `RuntimeError` with guidance that it is only usable during an active request, such as inside a view function.
`copy_current_request_context` now uses the same clearer request-context guidance when invoked without an active request context.
Out-of-context misuse no longer surfaces an incidental internal attribute-access failure for `after_this_request`.
acceptance_criteria: When `after_this_request` is called without an active request context, it should raise `RuntimeError` rather than an attribute-access exception.
When `after_this_request` fails due to missing request context, the error should clearly indicate that the decorator is only valid while handling a request, such as within a view function.
When `copy_current_request_context` is called without an active request context, it should raise `RuntimeError` with the same usage guidance as `after_this_request`.
When either decorator is used during an active request context, its existing successful behavior should remain unchanged.
